newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey PM says Israeli ties depend on behaviour.
newsitem.headline: Turkey PM says Israeli ties depend on behaviour.

text.p: Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, a persistent critic of Israel, on Tuesday linked improved ties with the Jewish state to its handling of the status of Jerusalem and its withdrawal from occupied lands.

Erbakan used a meeting with visiting Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy to demand immediate halt to construction of Jewish settlements and a pull-back by Israeli forces from the West Bank and Gaza strip.
"It is natural, as with all other countries, that developing our relations with Israel is part of our programme," he told reporters before meeting Levy.

"In this connection, Israel also has large responsibilities. ...Above all it must always recognise that Jerusalem is a sacred city for all peoples...for Muslims as well as for Christians and Jews," Erbakan said.
Israel must also halt the construction of new Jewish settlements in and around Jerusalem and withdraw from the occupied lands, in line with U.N. resolutions, he said.
Israeli soldiers and Jewish settlers shot dead three Palestinians and wounded 103 in West Bank clashes on Tuesday.

The clashes erupted after a Jewish settler shot dead a 24-year-old Arab shopkeeper in volatile Hebron, in the bloodiest day of violence since Israel launched construction on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem last month.
Levy, however, struck a more optimistic note.
"Another step has been taken in relations between the two countries," he said. "I believe in the future these relations will develop further."
Their meeting, which lasted for 45 minutes, ended days of speculation over whether Erbakan -- who campaigned against Turkish military ties to Israel -- would receive Levy at all.
Erbakan finally agreed on Monday to see the Israeli envoy.
His reticence, rooted in domestic politics and ideological affinities with Israel's Arab rivals, provoked an angry outburst from the Israeli embassy in Ankara.

Levy made clear he hoped to smooth relations with Erbakan and his Islam-based Welfare Party in a bid for political ties more in line with the warm military relations and growing commercial links the two countries already enjoy.
Erbakan won a slim plurality in 1995 general elections after campaigning to renounce a military training pact and other accords with Israel.
Under the deals, Israeli jets train over the Anatolian heartland, minutes from Israel's longtime rival Syria. Israel is also upgrading Turkey's ageing F-4 jets.
The deals angered much of the Moslem world and some Islamists in Turkey. They remain in effect despite Welfare's public opposition. Turkey's secularist generals insist they stay.

At the same time, commercial relations have grown steadily. Turkey is Israel's largest Middle East trading partner, with 1996 turnover estimated by the Israelis at $450 million. That figure could quadruple by the year 2000, they say, under a free trade pact approved by the Turkish parliament last week.
Levy also met Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller of the coalition's secularist wing and President Suleyman Demirel. On Wednesday Levy flies to Istanbul to meet Jewish leaders.
